MARKET OVERVIEW
🌎 A Fed Shock, an FCC Fight Over Iridium, and a SpaceX That Weathered Both

Track every space stock live at Orbit Alpha

The week was dominated by two overlapping stories: a hawkish Jackson Hole speech from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh that pushed September rate-hike odds from 35% to 57% and hit rate-sensitive, capital-intensive space names hard, and a regulatory skirmish between SpaceX and Iridium tied to Rocket Lab's pending $8 billion Iridium acquisition. SpaceX itself sat at the center of both stories and still finished the week higher, while most of the rest of the sector sold off.

SpaceX (SPCX)

SpaceX closed the week as the sector's clear outlier, up roughly 3.3% from last Friday's close ($136.97) to $141.50, even as the Fed speech and the Iridium regulatory flare-up hit almost everything else. The resilience traces to the market having now absorbed two consecutive post-IPO lockup tranches (911.5 million shares on August 6, another 319 million on August 20) without lasting damage, and to short sellers continuing to retreat. NASDAQ-settlement data tracked by MarketBeat showed shares short falling from 207.78 million (July 31 settlement) to 184.4 million (August 14 settlement), with days-to-cover collapsing from roughly 3 to 3.7 days down to about 1.2; S3 Partners separately pegged short interest at around 11% of tradable float by August 12, down from a 34% peak roughly a week earlier. On top of that, SpaceX generated a run of its own headlines. On August 25, Musk said SpaceX and Nvidia have co-designed a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 system for orbital AI compute, pulling the first orbital data-center launch forward to Q4 2027 from a previously stated 2028 target, news that sent the stock up about 3% that day to $139.06. JPMorgan's Doug Anmuth responded the next day, August 26, reiterating his Overweight rating and $240 price target (first set August 7) and pointing to improved prospects for SpaceX's Grok AI effort following the Cursor acquisition. Separately on August 25, SpaceX unveiled a second Starbase, a roughly $100 billion buildout in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana expected to bring about 3,000 direct jobs over a decade, with a first launch targeted for 2029; Musk said the Gulf Coast site would let the company "retire the Falcon rockets once Starship is flying multiple times per week." On August 28, Musk separately projected SpaceX could hit $3.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2033, recirculating Morgan Stanley's own Street-high $300 price target, first set in mid-July. That same day, SpaceX itself became a central actor in this week's other big story, filing an FCC complaint against Iridium over its conduct in the regulatory review of Rocket Lab's pending acquisition of Iridium (more below). Separately, Bloomberg and CNBC reported August 29 that OpenAI plans to cut off model access to Cursor, the coding-assistant startup SpaceX acquired for roughly $60 billion in a deal that closed August 14, effective November 12. It's a story worth watching but not yet stock-moving.

Rocket Lab (RKLB)

It was a heavy regulatory-paperwork week for Rocket Lab's pending $8 billion acquisition of Iridium. On August 24, the company filed an amended S-4/A confirming deal terms: Iridium holders get $27.00 cash plus a variable share allotment of Rocket Lab stock, collared between 0.24 and 0.40 shares depending on RKLB's price, backed by a $3.6 billion bridge facility and a $223.62 million termination fee, with a stockholder vote set for September 24 and closing expected mid-2027. The SEC declared the registration effective just after midnight on August 27. Then, later on August 28, SpaceX filed a complaint asking the FCC to scrutinize Iridium's conduct during the merger review, alleging Iridium has filed more than 50 petitions in eight months against rival satellite operators and raising a spectrum-interference dispute over next-generation Starlink gateways in shared bands. SpaceX said it does not oppose the deal itself, but the news still knocked RKLB down about 6% to $63.82 that day. Trefis analysts separately tracked a seven-straight-session slide (roughly -19%, through August 27, overlapping most of this week) and flagged Rocket Lab's own roughly -29% operating margin as a compounding, company-specific concern layered on top of the regulatory and macro pressure. Measured Friday-close to Friday-close, RKLB finished the week down about 11.3%, at $64.39.

Redwire (RDW)

Redwire had its busiest news stretch of the month packed into two days, even as the stock still fell about 9.6% amid the broader risk-off mood. On August 24, Redwire launched "Seeker," a new European-manufactured line of space cameras and navigation sensors (a 5-megapixel camera, a sub-5-arcsecond star tracker, and a quad sun sensor) built in Riga, Latvia, aimed at European supply-chain sovereignty. The next day, August 25, brought two more announcements: a licensing partnership with Luxembourg's Edge Aerospace to manufacture its space-qualified data-processing units and network switches at Redwire's Marlborough, Massachusetts facility, with first deliveries targeted for Q1 2027, and a strategic investment in next-generation phased-array antenna technology for LEO/MEO/GEO connectivity, building on the company's earlier Link-16-from-space military demonstrations.

MDA Space (MDA.TO)

MDA Space announced on August 27 the launch of "MDA Space LaunchPad Ventures," a new strategic investment program run in partnership with 49North targeting Canadian small and mid-sized companies developing space and defense technology across 25 identified focus areas; no fund size was disclosed. The stock still slipped roughly 5.9% in Toronto trading, in line with the sector-wide pullback.

Spire Global (SPIR)

Spire posted two government awards this week as part of NOAA's broader TMATE program: a roughly €4 million EUMETSAT renewal for radio-occultation weather data on August 25, and, on August 26, a $27.9 million, two-year NOAA contract to mature a hyperspectral microwave sounder payload toward flight readiness by 2030, alongside a separate $3 million NOAA extension for its existing HyMS demonstrator evaluation. Even so, SPIR closed the week down about 5.5% to $13.17, as the broader selloff outweighed the contract news.

Takeaway

Two overlapping stories defined this week: a hawkish Fed speech that repriced rate-hike odds and hit every leveraged, pre-profit name in the sector at once, and a SpaceX-versus-Iridium regulatory skirmish that put fresh, deal-specific risk on Rocket Lab's $8 billion Iridium acquisition. SpaceX itself sat at the center of both stories yet came out of the week higher. Next week's catalysts: Planet Labs reports fiscal Q2 earnings September 3; SpaceX's next lockup tranche (roughly 319 million shares) is expected around September 9, alongside a smaller Rule 144 affiliate tranche around September 10; and watch for any FCC response or further filings in the Iridium docket ahead of Rocket Lab and Iridium shareholders' September 24 vote.

DEEP DIVE
🎯 SPECTRUM WARS: HOW SPACEX'S FCC COMPLAINT PUT FRESH RISK ON ROCKET LAB'S $8 BILLION IRIDIUM DEAL

The space sector's biggest consolidation move of the year hit its first real regulatory turbulence this week, and the company that caused it was SpaceX, which is not even a party to the deal.

The Deal

Rocket Lab announced its acquisition of Iridium Communications on June 29, 2026, in a cash-and-stock transaction valued at roughly $8 billion, with Rocket Lab shares popping about 16% and Iridium's soaring about 25% that day, per CNBC. The strategic logic is straightforward: Rocket Lab gets a fully operational, 66-satellite low-Earth-orbit constellation with 2.5 million paying subscribers, $871.7 million in 2025 revenue, and a 57% operating EBITDA margin, plus, critically, Iridium's globally licensed L-band spectrum, without having to build a network from scratch. It pairs Rocket Lab's launch vehicles and satellite manufacturing with an active, cash-generative service business for the first time, and gives the company's in-development Neutron rocket a built-in anchor customer for constellation replenishment.

The Fine Points

On August 24, Rocket Lab filed an amended S-4/A registration statement spelling out the final mechanics. Iridium shareholders receive $27.00 in cash per share plus a variable allotment of Rocket Lab stock, with the exchange ratio collared between 0.4000 shares (if RKLB trades at or below $67.50) and 0.2400 shares (if RKLB trades at or above $112.50), calculated off a 10-day volume-weighted average price ending two trading days before closing. The cash portion is backed by a $3.6 billion committed bridge facility, and Iridium would owe a $223.62 million termination fee under specified walk-away scenarios. Iridium's stockholder vote is scheduled for September 24, with the deal expected to close by mid-2027 (extendable to December 2027) pending FCC and other regulatory clearances. The SEC declared the registration statement effective just after midnight on August 27.

Regulatory Risk

Even before this week's news, industry analysts were watching the FCC angle closely. Quilty Space's Caleb Henry noted Rocket Lab gains a "long-sought constellation" while Iridium gets access to vertical integration for its next satellite generation. ABI Research's Rachel Kong pointed to the deal's stable, high-margin government and enterprise customer base and access to scarce mobile-satellite-service spectrum as the core rationale. But PwC France's Mathieu Luinard was the most explicit about the risk. Rocket Lab, he said, "will have to manage dozens of jurisdictions' relationships to secure licenses and market-access renewals from the likes of the FCC or European regulators," even as the spectrum access itself represents what he called a "30-year moat" once secured.

Regulatory Risk Turned Concrete

SpaceX filed a complaint asking the FCC to examine Iridium's conduct during its review of the Rocket Lab transaction. SpaceX satellite policy associate Matthew Turk wrote that "Iridium's well-documented history of anticompetitive attacks against its competitors and American consumers hangs as a cloud over the proposed transaction," alleging Iridium had filed more than 50 petitions in eight months seeking to block or restrict rival satellite deployments. The specific dispute concerns SpaceX's next-generation Starlink gateways, which Iridium has argued could interfere with its own operations in the shared 19.4-19.6 GHz and 29.1-29.3 GHz bands "by a wide margin." Turk was careful to note SpaceX does not oppose the Rocket Lab-Iridium deal itself; it wants Iridium's broader regulatory conduct reviewed by the FCC. That nuance matters, because it makes this look less like an attempt to block the merger outright and more like SpaceX using the review process as leverage in an unrelated spectrum-interference dispute with Iridium.

Market Reaction

Within hours of the filing (reported at 2:02pm ET), Rocket Lab fell about 6% to $63.82, Intuitive Machines dropped about 5% to $15.32, and AST SpaceMobile slid about 6% to $58.04, all three explicitly linked to the news by multiple outlets, including 24/7 Wall St and Foreign Policy Journal. Even the Procure Space ETF (UFO), a diversified fund of small-cap space names, dipped about 2% that day. The reaction is a reminder of why the deal's variable exchange ratio matters beyond Rocket Lab's own stock price. Because Iridium holders' payout is tied to a VWAP calculated just before closing, anything that depresses or adds volatility to RKLB's share price in the run-up to a 2027 close directly changes what Iridium shareholders actually receive, even if the FCC ultimately clears the transaction without incident.

Why This Fits a Bigger Pattern. 

This is the second multibillion-dollar consolidation move to reshape the sector this summer, after SpaceX's roughly $60 billion acquisition of coding-assistant startup Cursor closed August 14. Between the two deals, the space sector's largest players are visibly moving from pure launch-and-satellite plays toward vertically integrated platforms, and, in SpaceX's case, into adjacent software businesses entirely. That shift raises the regulatory surface area these companies expose themselves to, whether it's spectrum allocation, antitrust scrutiny, or, in Cursor's case, AI-model licensing disputes with a partner like OpenAI. Rocket Lab's Iridium deal is the clearest test case so far of how much friction that consolidation wave will actually generate before deals reach the closing table.

Takeaway. Nothing filed this week changes the fundamental economics of the Rocket Lab-Iridium deal, and SpaceX's own framing suggests it isn't trying to kill the transaction. But the episode is a concrete illustration of execution risk that had, until now, been mostly theoretical analyst commentary. Watch the FCC docket for Iridium's response, watch whether other satellite operators pile on with similar petitions given Iridium's history, and watch Rocket Lab's stock price specifically in the weeks leading into any VWAP measurement window. In a deal structured like this one, regulatory noise and shareholder payout are now directly linked.
